Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural forces that civil engineers must contend with. When seismic waves pass through the ground, they impose complex lateral and vertical forces on structures that most buildings do not experience during normal service life. The collapse of buildings during earthquakes is rarely the result of a single factor. It typically stems from a combination of design shortcomings, construction deficiencies, soil conditions, and structural irregularities that compound one another under seismic loading. Understanding these failure mechanisms is essential. Historical case studies show that poor construction management has contributed to many catastrophic failures, as discussed in our article on
an overview of three important cases of building collapse due to poor construction management
.
Foundation Failures and Soil Liquefaction
One of the most insidious causes of earthquake-induced collapse is soil liquefaction. This phenomenon occurs when loose, water-saturated granular soil temporarily loses its strength and stiffness due to the rapid shaking of an earthquake. The pore water pressure rises until soil particles lose contact with one another, and the ground behaves more like a liquid than a solid. Buildings on liquefiable soils can sink, tilt, or suffer catastrophic foundation failure even during moderate seismic events. Properly designed
masonry walls help prevent failure and collapse
by providing lateral resistance, but they are only effective when the foundation system remains intact.
Soil liquefaction poses a particularly dangerous threat to pile foundations. When intermediate soil layers beneath the ground undergo liquefaction, piles that were designed to transfer loads through those layers suddenly lose lateral support. This induces additional bending moments and shear forces in the pile shaft that the reinforcement may not have been designed to resist. The failure can go unnoticed during visual inspections because the damage occurs deep below the ground surface. Geotechnical borehole investigations are the primary tool for identifying liquefaction risk, but the designer must interpret the data correctly and specify appropriate mitigation measures.
Several strategies reduce the risk of liquefaction-induced foundation failure:
Conducting thorough subsurface investigations with boreholes extending below all potentially liquefiable layers
Improving soil density through compaction grouting or vibro-compaction techniques
Installing stone columns or deep drainage systems to dissipate excess pore pressure
Extending pile foundations through liquefiable layers into competent bearing strata
Designing pile reinforcement to accommodate additional bending moments from liquefied soil layers
The interaction between the soil, the pile foundation, and the superstructure must be analyzed together to capture the true system behavior during an earthquake. Ignoring soil-pile-structure interaction is a common oversight that can lead to unexpected failure modes.
Short Column Effect and Soft Story Irregularities
The short column effect is one of the most frequently observed causes of structural damage in reinforced concrete frame buildings during earthquakes. A short column has an effective height significantly less than that of other columns in the same frame. Although the structural frame may have uniform column heights, the presence of partition walls, mezzanine beams, or sloping ground can reduce the effective clear height of certain columns. When lateral loads are applied, all columns at a given floor level must undergo the same lateral deflection. The short column, being stiffer, attracts a disproportionately higher share of the lateral force. This concentration of force can exceed the column’s shear capacity, leading to brittle shear failure. The
FIU bridge collapse investigation showed that dismissed safety concerns about structural behavior can have tragic consequences
, highlighting why early identification of such vulnerabilities is critical.
Common situations that create short columns include:
Buildings constructed on sloping ground, where the column height on the uphill side is shorter than on the downhill side
Intermediate beams cast between columns at mid-height to support stair landings or mezzanine floors
Brick or block partition walls built tight against columns, reducing the unsupported column length on one side
Sunken slabs or raised floor sections that alter the effective story height locally
Soft story irregularity is another common failure mode. A soft story has significantly lower lateral stiffness compared to the floors above or below it. In residential buildings, the ground floor is often kept open for parking or commercial space, with few partition walls to contribute lateral stiffness. The upper floors have numerous masonry infill walls that make them much stiffer. During an earthquake, the flexible ground floor undergoes excessive lateral deformation while the stiff upper floors remain relatively rigid. This creates a kinematic mechanism that concentrates damage at the soft story level, often resulting in partial or total collapse.
Overturning of Buildings and Pile Cap Failures
Buildings can overturn during earthquakes through two primary mechanisms: soil bearing failure and the P-Delta effect. Soil bearing failure occurs when cyclic vertical and horizontal shaking imposes stresses on the foundation soil that exceed its ultimate bearing capacity. When one side of a shallow foundation loses support due to soil bearing failure, the building begins to tilt. This tilt shifts the center of gravity, increasing the overturning moment in a self-reinforcing loop that can lead to complete toppling. The risk is especially high for buildings with narrow footprints or heavy roof systems. Understanding
earthquake resistance strategies for small buildings
is important because these structures are often more vulnerable to overturning due to their lower weight and reduced foundation dimensions.
The P-Delta effect is a second-order phenomenon that amplifies lateral deflections caused by earthquake shaking. As a building sways, vertical gravity loads act through an increasingly eccentric lever arm relative to the base. This eccentricity generates additional overturning moments not present in the original un-deformed configuration. In buildings that suffer permanent deformations during an earthquake, the load center shifts permanently, creating residual eccentricities that further reduce stability. The combination of excessive lateral deflection and gravity-induced secondary moments can push the structure beyond its point of instability.
Pile cap failures are another consequence of severe lateral loading. At the connection between piles and the pile cap, seismic forces can cause failure because the pile cap and ground beams form a very stiff assembly while the piles themselves are relatively slender. The connection becomes the weak link. When the superstructure sways, piles are forced to rotate and bend at their connection to the pile cap. If the reinforcement detailing at this junction is inadequate, the connection fails and the structural support system is lost. Soil-structure interaction at this interface can worsen the situation, as the surrounding soil imposes additional constraints on pile head movement.
Torsional Irregularities and Ductility Requirements
Irregularities in floor plan layout and stiffness distribution can introduce torsional behavior that causes disproportionate damage during earthquakes. When the center of mass and the center of stiffness do not coincide, lateral forces produce rotation in addition to translation. Structural engineers aim to have the first two vibration modes of a building be purely translational, avoiding the dominance of torsional modes. However, asymmetrical arrangements of shear walls, cores, and frames make this difficult. The side of the building that is more flexible experiences larger lateral deflections than the stiffer side, placing additional demands on the columns and walls in the flexible zone. Understanding
progressive collapse mechanisms in structures
is essential because a local failure triggered by torsional effects can propagate throughout the entire building.
The following table summarizes the key differences between regular and irregular structural configurations under seismic loading:
Parameter
Regular Configuration
Irregular Configuration
Center of mass vs. stiffness

Ductility is the ability of a structure to undergo large inelastic deformations without losing load-carrying capacity. Brittle structures absorb little energy before failure, while ductile structures dissipate significant seismic energy through controlled yielding. The ductility of a reinforced concrete structure depends almost entirely on reinforcement detailing. Special seismic detailing requirements for beam-column joints, confinement zones, and lap splices must be followed strictly. The plastic hinge regions near beam-column connections are particularly critical. These zones experience cyclic stress reversals during an earthquake, and the reinforcement detailing must prevent shear failure while allowing controlled flexural yielding. Inadequate transverse reinforcement in these areas can lead to sudden loss of vertical load capacity.
Lateral Stiffness and Foundation Settlement Considerations
Lateral stiffness is the resistance a structure offers against horizontal displacement. Buildings that lack adequate lateral stiffness experience excessive drifts that damage non-structural elements, induce P-Delta effects, and cause discomfort to occupants. The lateral load resisting system typically consists of moment-resisting frames, shear walls, or a combination of both. When shear walls are present, the interaction between the frame and the shear wall system can be considered in design to enhance overall capacity. However, the benefits are only realized when the shear walls are correctly positioned and have sufficient wall area to resist applied loads. Incorrect placement can increase torsional irregularities rather than reducing them. Engineers should review various
earthquake resistant design approaches
to select the most appropriate lateral system for each project.
Excessive settlement during earthquakes is closely linked to soil liquefaction and the presence of highly compressible soils. When loose or untreated soils are subjected to seismic shaking, they undergo volumetric compaction that manifests as ground surface settlement. If the soil beneath only part of a building settles, differential settlement occurs, leading to structural distress. In extreme cases, unbalanced soil capacities combined with ground shaking can cause the building to overturn. The liquefaction of internal soil layers can produce settlement of the overlying soil strata together with the building foundation, creating a sinking effect that damages the superstructure.
Key considerations for mitigating settlement and lateral stiffness problems include:
Performing site-specific seismic hazard analyses rather than relying on generic code values
Verifying that the selected lateral force resisting system provides adequate stiffness in both orthogonal directions
Ensuring soil improvement techniques address both bearing capacity and liquefaction potential
Using deep foundations that extend through compressible and liquefiable layers to stable bearing strata
Incorporating regular structural inspections into the building maintenance schedule
The design and construction of earthquake-resistant buildings requires a holistic understanding of geotechnical and structural engineering principles. No single measure is sufficient. Soil conditions, structural configuration, material quality, reinforcement detailing, and construction supervision all play interdependent roles in how a building performs when the ground begins to shake. A thorough grasp of
earthquake resistant design principles
is the foundation upon which safe, resilient structures are built. By learning from past failures and applying proven engineering methods, civil engineers can significantly reduce the risk of structural collapse during future seismic events.
